Getting approved for crypto payment processing doesn’t always mean merchants have full access to their revenue. This article explains why processors may impose rolling reserves due to chargeback exposure, volatility, fraud risk, and the perceived risk of crypto transactions, and what merchants can do to reduce reserve requirements and improve cash flow.

posts.reason: Rolling reserves and chargeback risk in crypto payments is tangentially relevant to our compliance and AML work, but this post targets merchant acquirers rather than our core buyer profiles.

comments.text: Worth adding that rolling reserves also function as a de facto forensic buffer for processors — the hold period is often what lets them catch chargeback patterns before funds are irreversibly moved on-chain. Once crypto proceeds hit a mixer or bridge, that reserve window closes fast.
Do processors typically disclose how reserve calculations weight on-chain risk signals versus traditional chargeback history, or is that still a black box for merchants?
We see the downstream side of this: when reserves are too thin or released too early, tracing fraudulent crypto payouts after the fact is far harder than catching them during the hold period.

posts.author: Private Financial Services

❗️ The first MiCA penalty: a signal for the entire EU crypto market

Austria's regulator (FMA) has fined crypto platform Bitpanda €70,000. It's the country's first published final penalty under MiCA — and a key precedent for the whole European Union.
What's telling: the target wasn't an obscure offshore newcomer, but one of Europe's largest and fully licensed players, headquartered in Vienna.

The specifics:
🔵 the white paper was filed late (MiCA requires it at least 20 working days before publication)
🔵 marketing went out before the white paper was published, and without mandatory disclosures and contact details

⭐️ It's important to note: this isn't fraud, and no client funds were lost. Bitpanda's license is unaffected, and so are customer assets. The breaches were purely procedural — "timing and formalities."

Regulation in the EU has shifted from "getting a license" to continuous compliance supervision. It's no longer just market entry under scrutiny, but every white paper, every marketing communication, every filing deadline.
For a crypto business, that means one thing: a license isn't the finish line — it's the start. What follows is a working compliance framework that keeps you from tripping on the "small things" that cost tens of thousands of euros.

posts.title: Neobanks that built in-house payment routing three years ago are now the ones shopping for orchestration platforms.
posts.author: Bryan Aaron
posts.snippet:
Neobanks that built in-house payment routing three years ago are now the ones shopping for orchestration platforms.

The architecture that made sense when you had two card networks and one bank partner stops scaling when you add crypto rails, local payment methods in twelve markets, and real-time settlement windows that do not wait for your ops team to wake up. The engineering team that could maintain custom routing logic for fiat cannot also rebuild fraud scoring, liquidity management, and fallback cascades every time a new settlement rail goes live.

What changed is not the cost of building. It is the cost of maintaining what you built. A unified gateway that handles both crypto and fiat through one API collapses that technical debt before it becomes the thing slowing every product decision.

The neobanks moving fastest right now are the ones willing to rip out the homegrown stack they were proud of two years ago.

Are you still running routing logic you wrote before stablecoins mattered?

posts.title: 🔵 Ethereum Layer 2: What Are Rollups? — Part 3
posts.author: Emtiyaz Onchain
posts.snippet:
🔵 Ethereum Layer 2: What Are Rollups? — Part 3

In my previous posts, I explored the basics of Layer 2 and then went deeper into Bitcoin’s Lightning Network.

Today, I’m continuing the series with Ethereum Layer 2 and Rollups.

Why does Ethereum need Layer 2?

Ethereum has limited blockspace.

When many users interact with the network at the same time:

More Activity → More Blockspace Demand → Higher Fees / Congestion

Layer 2 solutions try to handle more activity efficiently without requiring everything to happen directly on Ethereum Layer 1.

What is a Rollup?

A Rollup is a scaling approach where many transactions are processed on Layer 2 and information about those transactions is submitted to Ethereum Layer 1.

The important part is how Ethereum verifies that the Layer 2 activity is correct.

This leads to two major types of Rollups:

🟢 Optimistic Rollups

Optimistic Rollups generally assume that the submitted result is correct unless someone challenges it.

If someone believes the result is incorrect, a fraud/fault proof mechanism can be used to challenge it.

Simply:

Assume valid → Challenge if incorrect → Verify

🔵 ZK Rollups

ZK Rollups use cryptographic validity proofs to demonstrate that the Layer 2 computation was performed correctly.

Simply:

Process transactions → Generate proof → Submit proof → Ethereum verifies

⚙️ What is a Sequencer?

A Sequencer is a component used by many Layer 2 systems to receive transactions, order them, and help process them before submitting the relevant information to Ethereum.

A simplified flow:

Users → Sequencer → L2 Processing → Batch → Ethereum L1

Sequencer design is also important when thinking about the decentralization and security of an L2.

🧠 The simplest way to remember

Ethereum L1 → Main Blockchain / Settlement

Ethereum L2 → Scaling Layer

Rollup → Process many transactions on L2 and interact with Ethereum L1 using data and/or proofs

And:

Optimistic Rollup → Fraud/Fault Proof

ZK Rollup → Validity Proof

One thing I’ve noticed while learning these concepts is that topics like Rollups, Proofs, Sequencers, and Layer 2 security can be difficult to fully understand from short social media posts.

That’s why I’m also building a Web3 learning community on Discord, where we can go deeper into Blockchain, Crypto and Web3 topics, ask questions, discuss concepts, and learn together.

This is Part 3 of my Layer 2 learning series.

posts.title: 💶 Stablecoins are moving from hype to utility.
posts.author: INXY Payments
posts.snippet:
💶 Stablecoins are moving from hype to utility.
That is one of the clearest messages from The Paypers Global Stablecoins Report 2026.

The 73-page report looks at enterprise adoption, cross-border payments, liquidity, regulation, merchant payments, fraud, AML, and the infrastructure forming around stablecoins.

A few findings stood out to us.

1. Businesses are getting ready to use stablecoins.
Enterprise awareness is already close to universal, while actual production use remains much lower. But more than half of current non-users surveyed expect to start using stablecoins within the next 6–12 months.

The conversation is shifting from:
“Should we use stablecoins?”
to:
“Where should we use them first?”

2. Cross-border B2B looks like the natural starting point.
Supplier payments, international B2B transactions, and treasury flows are among the leading enterprise use cases.

The reason is simple.
Traditional cross-border payments can still mean several intermediaries, banking hours, slow settlement, and trapped liquidity.

Stablecoins can move 24/7 and settle much faster.
Not because blockchain is exciting.
Because the old process often is not.

3. The value goes beyond speed.
Among organisations already using stablecoins, 41% report savings of 10% or more compared with traditional payment methods.

But the bigger benefit may be control.
Less pre-funding. Better cash flow timing. More visibility. Fewer banking cut-off times.

For a CFO, that can matter more than shaving a few minutes off a transaction.

4. Stablecoins will not replace every payment rail.
This may be our favorite conclusion from the report.

The future is likely multi-rail.
Bank transfers, instant payments, cards, and stablecoins can exist side by side.

The real question is not:
“Will stablecoins replace banks?”
It is:
“Which rail works best for this payment?”
And this leads to the bigger story.

The hard part is no longer simply moving a token from A to B.
Businesses still need liquidity, fiat connectivity, conversion, AML, KYT, reconciliation, accounting, and settlement.

Stablecoins are becoming less of a crypto product and more of a piece of financial infrastructure.

We see the same shift at INXY Payments.
Our clients rarely come to us because they simply want crypto.
They want better ways to accept money, convert funds, automate payouts, and operate internationally. Stablecoins are becoming one of the rails that can make those flows work better.

These are only a few highlights from a much broader report.

The full 73-page Global Stablecoins Report 2026 by The Paypers goes much deeper into adoption, regulation, liquidity, merchant payments, orchestration, fraud, AML, and the future of stablecoin infrastructure.

posts.title: Financial crime increasingly looks less like a group of criminals and more like a service ecosystem.
posts.author: Alberto Remonti
posts.snippet:
Financial crime increasingly looks less like a group of criminals and more like a service ecosystem.

One actor sells stolen identities. Another provides scam infrastructure. Someone else recruits mules, moves the money or converts it into crypto.

The important part for investigators is that these actors may never appear connected on the surface.

That is why looking at individual accounts or transactions can miss the wider picture.

The real question is not only who moved the money, but who provided the services that made the crime possible.Follow the network, not just the transaction.
posts.reason: Financial crime as a service ecosystem and the importance of network analysis over isolated transactions is directly aligned with our forensics methodology and appeals to investigators and law enforcement.

comments.text: This matches what we see when tracing proceeds across chains: the mule network, the swap service and the off-ramp are often run by entirely separate actors who only interact through smart contracts or OTC desks, never directly. Mapping the service layer rather than the transaction chain is usually what actually identifies a cash-out point worth freezing.

When you map these service ecosystems, how do you weigh the evidentiary value of behavioural/infrastructure links (shared hosting, wallet clustering) against the higher bar prosecutors usually want, i.e. direct transactional links?

We've had cases where the identity theft, the mule recruitment and the crypto conversion were three unrelated groups on Telegram, coordinating without ever transacting with each other on-chain - only the exchange choke point tied the whole thing together.

If you're a founder still treating AI as a tool selection problem, you're solving the wrong question.

I've watched my own team cycle through multiple ChatGPT Pro accounts, then Plus accounts, then quietly migrate to better-fit tools as the landscape shifted. That migration wasn't random. It followed where capability actually lived. The same logic applies at a geopolitical scale, except the stakes aren't a $200 monthly subscription.

The Queensland crypto scam story this week is worth noting too. AI has already cut the administrative cost of running sophisticated fraud operations. The same infrastructure that scales legitimate business scales harm. That's always been true of electricity. Of the internet. The technology doesn't decide. The structure around it does.

Which platforms and partnerships are you building on right now, and have you thought about who controls them?

Litigation & Dispute Resolution ⚖️🚨

When fraud crosses borders, recovery often requires more than a complaint. Litigation and dispute resolution can create a binding legal pathway to pursue defendants, preserve assets, obtain disclosure, and enforce judgments.

Cross-border fraud litigation may involve civil claims, interim freezing orders, disclosure applications, settlement strategy, judgment enforcement, and coordinated action across multiple jurisdictions. ⚖️

🔍 Cases that may require litigation:
📈 Investment platform fraud
🪙 Crypto and blockchain fraud
📊 Forex, CFD, and broker fraud
💔 Pig butchering and romance scams
🏠 Real estate investment fraud
📦 Supplier and non-delivery fraud
🏢 Business acquisition fraud
📉 Ponzi schemes and collective investment fraud
🧾 Recovery fraud and clone firm scams

⚖️ Litigation options may include:
✔️ Jurisdiction analysis and forum selection
✔️ Pre-action evidence preparation
✔️ Civil claims for fraud, deceit, breach of contract, unjust enrichment, or fiduciary breach
✔️ Emergency freezing and asset preservation orders
✔️ Disclosure and Norwich Pharmacal applications
✔️ Multi-defendant claims against companies and beneficial owners
✔️ Settlement negotiation and dispute resolution
✔️ Cross-border judgment recognition and enforcement

🛡️ Strong litigation starts with:
📂 Contracts, payment records, invoices, emails, and screenshots
🔎 Defendant identification and company verification
💸 Transaction reconstruction and asset tracing
🌐 Jurisdiction strategy based on defendant location, asset location, and enforcement options
⚖️ Specialist litigation counsel in the correct forum

⏳ Speed matters. The earlier a case is prepared, the stronger the chance of preserving assets before defendants move funds, restructure companies, or disappear.

Recruitment Scam Series  #4: 
Telegram & WhatsApp Task / "Like & Rate" Scams:-

How It Works:-

Candidates receive unsolicited messages on WhatsApp, Telegram, or SMS offering flexible remote work (e.g., liking YouTube videos, reviewing Google locations, or rating products for ₹2,000–₹5,000 daily). Some even claim 150rupees or 50rupees per like so people believe it …

To build trust, scammers pay small real returns (₹150–₹500 via UPI) for the first few simple tasks. Next, they add the candidate to a Telegram group and introduce "VIP Prepaid Tasks" or "Crypto Investment Tasks." 

The candidate is persuaded to transfer money (from ₹1,000 up to lakhs) under the promise of massive returns. 

When the candidate tries to withdraw their "earnings," the scammers block them or demand even more money as "tax" or "unlocking fees."

Key Red Flags to Spot:-
 * Unsolicited messages offering lucrative daily income for basic tasks like liking posts or writing reviews.

 * Receiving initial small payouts via UPI to win your trust before asking for funds.

 * Being redirected to Telegram channels where admins pressure you to transfer money into crypto or unknown individual accounts.

Recruiter’s Advice to Candidates:-

A legitimate job pays you for your work,
you should NEVER have to invest or transfer money to complete a job task or withdraw your earned salary."

A few seconds later, someone did.

No obvious scam.

Just a friendly reply.

look foolish.

A good moderator creates an environment where reporting is easy and 
encouraged.

Because the earlier a problem is reported, the easier it is to stop.

In crypto, trust isn't only about solving big problems.

ones.

You can revoke credentials.

Week of August 24, 2026
This week, we are taking a closer look at one of the most stressful digital threats everyday users face: Ransomware.

Crypto Ransomware (File-Encrypting): Locks down individual files, photos, and documents.

Double-Extortion Ransomware: Encrypts your data and threatens to leak private files publicly if a ransom isn't paid.

Triple-Extortion Ransomware: Escalates threats by targeting your contacts or third parties using data stolen from your device.

Leakware / Doxware: Focuses on stealing sensitive personal information and threatening to publish it online.

Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS): A business model where cybercriminals lease ransomware tools to others, making attacks much more frequent.
  
Next week we will explore Crypto Ransomware in detail and see how we can combat this one.

🚚 Core Challenges for Logistics Coordinators

1. Transportation & Cost Pressures
Rising fuel and freight costs squeeze margins and require constant optimization.
Poor route planning or low vehicle utilization can quickly erode profitability.
Solution: Use Transportation Management Systems (TMS), conduct regular carrier audits, and optimize load consolidation.

2. Customs & Regulatory Compliance
Evolving rules and “digital borders” demand accurate documentation, pre‑lodgement, and audit trails.
Mistakes in filings can cause delays, fines, or shipment seizures.
Solution: Build compliance by design with clean master data, clear ownership of filings, and refresher training for staff.

3. Talent & Workforce Shortages
Shortage of drivers, warehouse labor, and digital skillsets.
High turnover and lack of specialized training increase operational risk.
Solution: Cross‑train teams, standardize SOPs, and invest in micro‑learning to keep skills fresh.

4. Visibility & Data Quality
Many operations still rely on fragmented spreadsheets and disconnected systems, leading to shipment visibility gaps.
This causes missed handoffs, damaged shipments, or late deliveries.
Solution: Integrate TMS/WMS/telematics into a single platform and establish governance for data ownership.

5. Customer Expectations
Service windows are shorter, and last‑mile logistics is under pressure.
Delays or damaged goods directly impact satisfaction and contracts.
Solution: Improve forecasting, strengthen communication with carriers, and use real‑time tracking tools.

6. Sustainability & ESG
Companies face carbon reporting and reduction targets.
Logistics coordinators must balance cost efficiency with measurable sustainability.
Solution: Route/load optimization, energy‑efficient equipment, and right‑sized packaging.

7. Cybersecurity & Resilience
Ransomware and IoT risks can halt operations.
Coordinators must ensure systems and partners are secure.
Solution: MFA, patching, least‑privilege access, and tabletop drills for crisis scenarios.

posts.title: Your hardware wallet's private keys were never touched. Your seed phrase is still safe. Your crypto is still secure.
posts.author: Willow Liu
posts.snippet:
Your hardware wallet's private keys were never touched. Your seed phrase is still safe. Your crypto is still secure.

Your home address is now in the hands of whoever bought it on a criminal forum.

On August 13, Trezor disclosed that a breach at its shipping partner, ShipMonk, exposed the names, phone numbers, and home addresses of roughly 13,700 customers — a list that, by definition, identifies exactly who owns a device built to protect meaningful crypto holdings, and exactly where to find them. Trezor's own systems were untouched. The attacker didn't need them. ShipMonk held SOC 2 Type II certification — an audited security standard — and got breached anyway.

This isn't a new playbook. Ledger's payment processor leaked customer order data in a nearly identical incident back in January. The pattern keeps repeating because the industry keeps treating "self-custody" as a purely digital problem, while the real attack surface has quietly moved into the supply chain: shipping labels, fulfillment vendors, and analytics platforms nobody outside IT has ever heard of.

And this isn't hypothetical risk. Researchers tracked 52 verified physical attacks on crypto holders in the first half of 2026, up from 39 in the same period last year, with home invasions now outpacing kidnapping as the most common method. One French couple who moved into a home previously owned by a known crypto holder were reportedly hit with three separate invasions in under a month. The address was the target, not the resident.

My hot take: the entire pitch of hardware wallets is "eliminate counterparty risk." Nobody in that pitch mentions that your new counterparty is a third-party logistics vendor now sitting on your GPS coordinates. "Not your keys, not your coins" was never the whole sentence. It should have ended with "...but definitely still your address."

If your platform ships anything physical to customers — devices, cards, onboarding kits — your vendor risk assessment needs to cover the fulfillment company, not just the payment processor. That's not paranoia. That's the current threat model.

I've spent my career on the platform-security and anti-fraud side of crypto trading, plus AML/risk experience from Alipay. If your team is rethinking vendor and supply-chain risk in light of incidents like this, I'd love to compare notes.

posts.title: Agents that spend money
posts.author: Sandeep More, PMP®
posts.snippet:
Agents that spend money

Problem tackled: agents can call paid APIs but have no bounded spending authority — teams hand them a shared key with no cap, so a retry loop becomes a billing incident nobody sees until the invoice.
Framework angle: x402 (HTTP 402 revived) as the protocol answer; AWS AgentCore Payments (GA 18 Aug 2026) enforcing limits at the infrastructure layer rather than in the prompt.

Your agent can call any API you gave it a key for. It cannot tell you how much that key is about to cost you.

We've spent two years getting good at what an agent may do. Tools, scopes, permissions, approval gates. We've barely started on how much it may spend.

Most teams solve it the same way: one shared API key, no cap, and hope.

That's fine until the agent loops. A stuck agent doesn't just burn tokens — every retry against a paid endpoint is a purchase. The failure doesn't show up in your logs. It shows up in the invoice, three weeks later.

There's a genuinely interesting fix moving right now, and it's older than it looks.

HTTP has had a 402 Payment Required status code sitting reserved and unused since the 1990s. The x402 protocol finally uses it. Request arrives without payment, server responds 402 with the price, the client pays, retries, gets the data. No account, no key, no monthly reconciliation.

In the last 30 days that network moved about $24M across roughly 75 million transactions. That's around 32 cents each — machine-scale payments, not human ones.

AWS put this in the platform on 18 August: AgentCore Payments went GA with x402 support and payment limits enforced at the infrastructure layer.

That last phrase is the whole engineering point. A spending rule in a system prompt is a suggestion. A spending rule in the runtime is a constraint. You wouldn't enforce rate limits inside code the model can influence — spend is no different.

The rails are stablecoin-based today, which plenty of enterprises won't touch, and that's fine. The transferable idea doesn't need crypto: every agent gets a budget, a per-call ceiling, and a hard stop that lives outside the model's reach.

If your agent went into a retry loop tonight against a paid API, what stops it — a limit, or the invoice?

posts.title: How do UK private investigators locate beneficiaries, debtors, old friends and missing people?
posts.author: UK Private Investigators
posts.snippet:
How do UK private investigators locate beneficiaries, debtors, old friends and missing people?

After 29 years of service to the private investigation industry, I’ve seen one thing remain constant: when someone needs to be found, the answer is rarely as simple as “just search online.”

UK private investigators use a combination of experience, research, open-source intelligence, specialist databases, public records and investigative techniques to establish where a person may be today.

The circumstances can vary considerably:

🔎 Beneficiary tracing — locating beneficiaries of estates, trusts or unclaimed assets when contact details are out of date.

💷 Debtor tracing — helping businesses and individuals establish current contact or address information where a debtor has disappeared or become difficult to reach.

🤝 Reconnecting with old friends — tracing someone from a previous chapter of your life when you have little more than a name, former address, workplace or other historical information.

📍 Missing people — establishing potential current whereabouts and, where appropriate, making contact through lawful and proportionate investigative methods.

The real skill is not simply finding information. It is connecting the right pieces of information, verifying them and understanding what they mean.

People change names, move home, change employment, disappear from social media and leave behind very little digital footprint. That’s where nearly three decades of industry experience can make a significant difference.

Of course, investigations must be conducted lawfully, ethically and with respect for privacy and data protection requirements. A professional investigator should understand not only how to trace someone, but also when and why certain information can legitimately be obtained and used.

After 29 years in the industry, I still find tracing work fascinating — because behind every enquiry there is usually a story, a reason for the search and someone who needs answers.

posts.author: Umang Someshwar

The direction of QFZP scrutiny is becoming clearer: the discussion is shifting from formal eligibility to the evidence of substance, commercial decision-making and underlying distribution activity.

For Free Zone distributors, the more difficult question may no longer be whether a 0% QFZP position can be articulated. The real question is whether the position can be demonstrated through the way the business is actually run and through the contemporaneous evidence available to support it.

A trade licence, Free Zone address, warehouse, employees and audited financial statements are all relevant. But they may not, by themselves, explain whether the distribution activity is genuinely conducted in or from the required Designated Zone, whether the relevant functions are performed through the Free Zone operating platform, or whether the customer and goods-flow conditions are met.

The practical focus therefore moves to questions such as:
Where are material supplier, pricing, credit, inventory and customer decisions made?
Who performs or controls the significant functions of the distribution business?
Where goods enter the UAE, can the import route be reconciled to customs, freight, inventory and sales records?
Can the business distinguish customers acquiring goods for resale, processing or alteration from end users?
Do the people, assets, expenditure, governance arrangements and related-party arrangements support the operating model described in the QFZP analysis?
Is the evidence being built throughout the year, or only reconstructed when the Corporate Tax return, AUP process or a review requires it?

These questions are particularly relevant because QFZP treatment is not simply a year-end tax conclusion. It is an operating position that needs to remain aligned with the underlying business model, revenue profile, governance and documented facts throughout the relevant Tax Period.

I have examined these issues in my recent FinTedu article, “Qualifying Free Zone Person: Substance and Distribution Activities — From Formal Conditions to Demonstrable Operating Reality.”

The article considers the QFZP framework for distribution activities alongside practical areas such as adequate substance, decision-making, goods flows, customer status, group operating models, outsourcing, AUP readiness and the documentation that can make an operating model visible.

Read the article here: https://lnkd.in/dsJfrPSj

On a few smaller venues it's insurance, an outside underwriter paid over the odds to stand behind a fund the members won't.

Four answers with different mechanics, and in all but the bluntest of them the loss stays inside the membership, just redistributed to a different corner of it.

Here's the fifth, the one that list never includes: securitise the tail. Price the exposure and transfer it to capital-market investors who actually want that risk. Instead of every member quietly underwriting every other member, the tail sits with whoever's paid to hold it.

It's not a free lunch. Pricing a tail event well is genuinely hard. Moral hazard doesn't disappear on its own. Investor appetite for this exact risk thins out right when stress hits. Still, it's an answer the industry hasn't had to reckon with before, mostly because it's only becoming feasible now.

What can a cryptocurrency wallet reveal during an investigation? 🔎
A crypto wallet is more than a place to hold digital assets. It can provide valuable on-chain and forensic clues.
Investigators may examine:
🔹 Wallet addresses & transaction history
🔹 Incoming/outgoing transfers & timestamps
🔹 Transaction patterns and relationships
🔹 Connected addresses
🔹 Token, NFT & smart-contract activity
🔹 Wallet files, backups & device artifacts
🔹 Links between on-chain activity and off-chain evidence
🕵️ Typical workflow:
Acquire → Extract → Trace → Correlate → Document
⚠️ A blockchain address does not automatically reveal a person's identity. Attribution usually requires correlation with additional evidence, such as exchange records, device artifacts, or other investigative data.
💡 The wallet may not tell you who someone is—but the transaction trail can provide valuable clues about where funds moved and how addresses are connected.

Market intelligence across crypto, foreign exchange and commodities, from a site that models volatility and refuses to pretend it can forecast direction.

What is knowable.

Volatility clusters, so a turbulent-or-calm classification carries measurable skill: about 66% correct at seven days and 73% at thirty in a five-year point-in-time backtest. Direction. The scorecard reads crypto 49 percent over 320 calls, commodities 62 percent over 90, and foreign exchange not yet scored. Crypto is the large sample and it sits almost exactly at chance. posts.title: Malaysia's new identity verification requirement for paid social media ads took effect on 1 June 2026, under the Risk Mitigation Code (RMC).
posts.author: Parseh PPC

Malaysia's new identity verification requirement for paid social media ads took effect on 1 June 2026, under the Risk Mitigation Code (RMC).

The rule applies to platforms with more than eight million users in Malaysia, including Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. Every advertiser, whether an individual or a registered company, must be verified against government-issued records before a sponsored post can be published.

The Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission introduced the requirement to address sponsored posts misusing the images of public figures to promote dubious investments, scams and online gambling. Non-compliant licensed platforms face financial penalties of up to RM10 million, though a transition period is currently in place.

The change is not limited to social media. Google introduced its own Financial Services Verification requirement for advertisers in Malaysia earlier in 2026, requiring businesses promoting loans, investments or similar products to prove they are authorised by regulators such as Bank Negara Malaysia.

For most legitimate businesses, the practical impact is procedural: keeping company registration records and valid identification on hand for when platforms request verification.

posts.title: 3 Ultimate Signs That an Investor Is a Scam
posts.author: Avie Marucot
posts.snippet:
3 Ultimate Signs That an Investor Is a Scam
Finding an investor can be exciting, especially when you’re trying to grow a business. But not everyone who promises funding is a legitimate investor. Some scammers deliberately target entrepreneurs who are eager to raise capital.
Here are 3 major warning signs to watch out for:
1. They Ask You to Pay Money Before You Receive the Investment
One of the biggest red flags is an “investor” who asks you to pay an upfront fee for processing, taxes, registration, legal fees, or releasing the funds.
Legitimate investors may conduct due diligence, but you should be extremely cautious if someone says:
“Pay this fee first, and we’ll release your investment.”
Never assume that a promised multimillion-peso investment is real simply because the person sends you documents or screenshots showing proof of funds.
2. They Promise Guaranteed Returns
Real investing involves risk. If someone guarantees that your business will earn a specific amount or promises an unusually high return with zero risk, be skeptical.
Statements such as:
“You are guaranteed to double your money.”
“There is absolutely no risk.”
“You will receive ₱1 million within 30 days.”
“You just need to send the money today.”
are serious warning signs.
A legitimate investor will generally want to understand your business, financials, market, risks, and growth potential before making an investment decision.
3. They Pressure You to Act Immediately
Scammers often create a sense of urgency so you don't have enough time to verify who they are.
Be careful if an investor says:
“This offer expires tonight.”
or
“Send your documents and payment now, or we’ll give the investment to someone else.”
A genuine investor should be willing to let you perform reasonable due diligence. Verify their identity, company registration, investment history, and professional background. If they claim to represent an investment firm, independently verify the firm through official sources rather than relying solely on contact information they provide.
The Golden Rule: Verify Before You Trust
Before accepting an investment, slow down and investigate.
Ask yourself:
Who are they? Where did their money come from? What is their investment history? What exactly are they asking from me? And why do they need money from me before investing in my business?
If something feels rushed, secretive, or too good to be true, take a step back.
A real investor wants to invest in your business. A scammer may be more interested in getting money, personal information, or control from you.
Do your due diligence before signing anything or sending money.

posts.title: Generative recommendation (GR) is rapidly becoming the dominant paradigm for recommender systems in the generative AI era. Yet almost all existing GR models are optimized purely fo
posts.author: Shoujin Wang
posts.snippet:
Generative recommendation (GR) is rapidly becoming the dominant paradigm for recommender systems in the generative AI era. Yet almost all existing GR models are optimized purely for accuracy, while overlooking a critical societal dimension: the credibility of the content they recommend. This blind spot can expose users to fake news and misinformation, eroding user trust, damaging platform reputation, and even contributing to broader social instability. To address this critical yet underexplored challenge, we are excited to present our latest work, "Generate What You Can Trust: Content Credibility in Generative Recommenders", accepted at EMNLP 2026 (CORE A*).

Highlights:
CreGR Framework: The first GR model to explicitly account for the credibility of generated recommendations — improving credibility while preserving high recommendation accuracy.
Credibility-aware Tokenizer: Introduces credibility regularization that disentangles credible and uncredible items at the discrete token level, so that topically similar but factually divergent items are no longer mapped to nearby tokens.
Accuracy-preserving and Credibility-oriented Generator: A discrete-diffusion generator with an asymmetric masking probability reduction strategy (hard and soft variants) that selectively suppresses uncredible token contributions while leaving user-preference signals untouched.

Practical Impact:
Our work has broad implications for end users and any platform where trust and content quality matter:

News & Social Media: Reduces the recommendation of fake news while still capturing users' genuine topical interests, helping to break the self-reinforcing filter bubbles and echo chambers that fake-news exposure creates.

Digital Health: Curbs the spread of health misinformation that users may act on, steering recommendations toward reliable health-related content without losing sight of the user's underlying interest in wellness topics.

Financial Services: Reduces exposure to misleading investment tips, scams, and unverified financial claims that users may act on with real monetary consequences, promoting safer and more trustworthy financial content recommendations.

Trustworthy & Responsible AI: Builds credibility directly into the recommendation model rather than filtering content after the fact, offering a principled foundation for the next generation of responsible generative recommenders.

posts.title: The ideology Nigeria hasn't named yet and why naming it is the most important economic task of the decade

The ideology Nigeria hasn't named yet and why naming it is the most important economic task of the decade
Every developmental state was built on a coherent, named economic ideology. Singapore's pragmatic capitalism. South Korea's state-directed industrialism. Botswana's resource nationalism. Nigeria is at the inflection point where its next ideology must be consciously chosen not stumbled into.

Nigeria's current economic operating system is unnamed and unexamined. Let's name it.

THE CURRENT SYSTEM: PETROLEUM-FUNDED PATRONAGE
The Nigerian state has operated for 60 years on a logic of petroleum revenue distribution through a patronage network. The federal government collects oil money and distributes it through FAAC allocations, contracts, and appointments. States compete for federal transfers rather than growing their own revenue bases. Citizens receive subsidies rather than services.

This system is structurally ending. Oil revenue is declining. The subsidy is gone. The FAAC allocation is shrinking in real terms. The patronage model is running out of fuel.

WHAT COMES NEXT?
At Vibranium Capital, our reading of Nigeria's political economy trajectory points to a hybrid model with four pillars:

1. Domestic capital mobilization: pension funds, diaspora remittances, and capital market deepening as the primary source of infrastructure investment not foreign aid or oil revenue.

2. African continental trade: positioning Nigeria as a manufacturing and services export hub for the ECOWAS and AfCFTA market ,1.3 billion people, zero tariffs.

3. Private sector-led service delivery: healthcare, education, logistics, and housing delivered primarily by regulated private operators with state co-financing.

4. Sub-national fiscal autonomy: states that build genuine IGR bases Lagos-model becoming the growth engines of the federation.

This ideology doesn't have a name yet. We call it developmental federalism. The investment theses we build are designed for the world it creates.

comments.text: Worth adding that for crypto-denominated POF the picture is even messier: an exchange balance screenshot proves nothing about the origin of the coins or whether they'd survive a source-of-funds check once withdrawn. We regularly see funds that are technically 'available' but trace back through mixers or sanctioned addresses, which kills the deal at the compliance stage rather than the financial one.

When you do this verification on crypto-linked capital, how far back do you typically trace the on-chain history before calling a source clean - one hop, or through to the original deposit into a regulated venue?

We see the mirror image of this in AML work: a bank letter confirming a balance that turned out to be freshly converted from crypto with no clean audit trail behind it. Availability and legitimacy really are two separate questions, and treating them as one is where most of the risk hides.
